collection: Microsoft Learn previous-versions, Windows CE 5.0 product documentation
note: Compiler behaviour documented for the Windows CE 5.0 compiler.
statement: If the packsize is set equal to or greater than the default alignment, the packsize is ignored. If the packsize is set smaller than the default alignment, the compiler aligns according to the packsize value. Thus, if the packsize is set to four, data types having a size of four, eight, or 16 bytes are aligned on addresses that are multiples of four.

collection: Microsoft Learn previous-versions, Windows Embedded CE 6.0 documentation
note: Same statement documented for Windows Embedded CE 6.0.
statement: If the packsize is set equal to or greater than the default alignment, the packsize is ignored. If the packsize is set smaller than the default alignment, the compiler aligns according to the packsize value. Thus, if the packsize is set to four, data types having a size of four, eight, or 16 bytes are aligned on addresses that are multiples of four.

collection: Microsoft Learn previous-versions, Windows CE 5.0 product documentation
note: Effect of the pack pragma on member alignment.
statement: For example, in a structure declared under #pragma pack(1) , the alignment of all members are forced to one, regardless of whether they would have been naturally aligned even without packing.

collection: Microsoft Learn previous-versions, Windows CE .NET 4.x documentation
note: Default structure member alignment.
statement: Ordinarily, when storage is allocated for structures, their members are DWORD -aligned using the default value, /Zp8 .

collection: Microsoft Learn previous-versions, Windows CE .NET 4.x documentation
note: Allowed pack sizes.
statement: When you select the /Zp n option, where n is 1, 2, 4, 8, or 16, each structure member after the first is stored on n -byte boundaries.

collection: Microsoft Learn previous-versions, Windows CE 5.0 product documentation
note: Documented alignment requirement and the __unaligned escape hatch.
statement: The __unaligned keyword is a type modifier in pointer definitions. It indicates to the compiler that the data pointed to might not be properly aligned on a correct address. To be properly aligned, the address of an object must be a multiple of the size of the type.

collection: Microsoft Learn previous-versions, Windows Embedded CE 6.0 documentation
note: Same statement documented for Windows Embedded CE 6.0.

collection: Microsoft Learn previous-versions, Windows CE 5.0 product documentation
note: What enters a linker name.
statement: By default, C++ uses the function name, parameters, and return type to create a linker name for the function.

collection: Microsoft Learn previous-versions, Windows CE 5.0 product documentation
note: Documented linker name for each calling convention and language form.
statement: Calling convention | extern "C" or .c file | .cpp, .cxx or /TP
C naming convention (__ cdecl ) | _test | ?test@@ZAXXZ
Fastcall naming convention (__ fastcall ) | @test@0 | ?test@@YIXXZ
Standard Call naming convention (__ stdcall ) | _test@0 | ?test@@YGXXZ

collection: Microsoft Learn previous-versions, Windows CE 5.0 product documentation
note: What a C++ decorated name encodes.
statement: The following information is contained in a decorated name for a C++ function: The function name The class that the function is a member of, if it is a member function This can include the class that encloses the function's class, and so on. The types of the function's parameters The calling convention The return type of the function The string contains the literal names of the function and class. The rest of the string is a code that has internal meaning only for the compiler and linker.

collection: Microsoft Learn previous-versions, Windows CE 5.0 product documentation
note: Documented example pairs of undecorated and decorated C++ names.
statement: Undecorated name | Decorated name
int a(char){int i=3;return i;}; | ?a@@YAHD@Z
void __stdcall b::c(float){}; | ?c@b@@QAGXM@Z

collection: Microsoft Learn previous-versions, Windows CE 5.0 product documentation
note: What a .def file is used for.
statement: A module-definition (.def) file is a text file that contains statements defining an executable (.exe) file or dynamic-link library (DLL). Although all executable files can use .def files, they are mainly used by the linker tool to create .exe files and DLL files as one of the final steps in the build process.

collection: Microsoft Learn previous-versions, Windows Embedded CE 6.0 documentation
note: Same topic for Windows Embedded CE 6.0.
statement: A module-definition (.def) file is a text file which contains statements defining the public symbols, functions and variables, that are exported from an executable file. The executable file is typically a dynamic-link library (DLL).

collection: Microsoft Learn previous-versions, Windows CE 5.0 product documentation
note: Linker option that consumes a .def file.
statement: This option passes a module-definition file (.def) to the linker. Only one .def file can be specified to LINK.

collection: Microsoft Learn previous-versions, Windows CE 5.0 product documentation
note: Entry name versus internal name.
statement: This option allows you to export a function from your program so that other programs can call the function. You can also export data.

collection: Microsoft Learn previous-versions, Windows CE 5.0 product documentation
note: Export ordinals and the NONAME keyword.
statement: The ordinal specifies an index into the exports table in the range 1 through 65,535; if you do not specify ordinal, LINK assigns one. The NONAME keyword exports the function only as an ordinal, without an entryname.

collection: Microsoft Learn previous-versions, Windows CE 5.0 product documentation
note: How a linker finds the library that provides a symbol.
statement: A library specified with /DEFAULTLIB is searched after libraries specified on the command line and before default libraries named in .obj files.

collection: Microsoft Learn previous-versions, Windows CE 5.0 product documentation
note: Byte-order rule stated for the Winsock service provider interface.
statement: A service provider should treat all sockaddr calls exclusive of the address family parameter as if they are in the network byte order, and the address family parameter as in the local machine's byte order.

collection: Microsoft Learn previous-versions, Windows CE 5.0 product documentation
note: Little-endian layout stated for a 32-bit registry value.
statement: In little-endian format, a multibyte value is stored in memory from the lowest byte (the little end) to the highest byte.

collection: Microsoft Learn previous-versions, Windows CE .NET 4.x documentation
note: Documented argument sizes for the ARM target.
statement: If integer and integer-equivalent arguments such as char or pointer are not larger than 32-bits, a calling function passes them as 32-bit words. If the argument is 64-bits, the function passes it as a 4-byte aligned scalar.

collection: Microsoft Learn previous-versions, Windows CE 5.0 product documentation
note: Documented stack frame allocation for the ARM target.
statement: A sequence of zero or more instructions that allocate the remaining stack frame space for local variables, compiler-generated temporaries, and the argument build area by subtracting a 4-byte aligned offset from R13 .

collection: Microsoft Learn previous-versions, Windows CE 5.0 product documentation
note: Documented stack frame allocation for the SH-4 target.
statement: A sequence of zero or more instructions that allocate the remaining stack frame space for local variables, compiler-generated temporaries, and the argument-build area by subtracting a 4-byte aligned offset from R15 .

collection: Microsoft Learn previous-versions, Windows CE 5.0 product documentation
note: Assembler directives that select the ARM instruction set.
statement: Directive | Description
CODE16 | Tells the assembler that subsequent instructions are to be interpreted as 16-bit (Thumb) instructions.
CODE32 | Tells the assembler that subsequent instructions are to be interpreted as 32-bit (ARM) instructions.

DATA | Tells the assembler that the label is a "data-in-code" label; that is, that it defines an area of data within a code segment. You must specify this directive if you are defining data in a Thumb code area.

collection: Microsoft Learn previous-versions, Windows Embedded CE 6.0 documentation
note: Default image entry points for DLLs and EXEs.
statement: For a DLL, the default entry point is _ DllMainCRTStartup . For an EXE, the default entry is wWinMainCRTStartup , the Unicode entry point for an EXE that defines the wWinMain function, or WinMainCRTStartup otherwise.

collection: Microsoft Learn previous-versions, Windows CE 5.0 product documentation
note: Documented stream-interface entry point naming, including the undecorated alternative.
statement: Device Manager uses the XXX prefix. When implementing the stream interface, replace XXX with a prefix appropriate for your specific implementation or use undecorated entry point names in conjunction with DEVFLAGS_NAKEDENTRIES.
